meadow.e: From Middle English medowe, medewe, medwe (also mede > Modern English mead), from Old English mǣdwe, inflected form of mǣd (see mead), from Proto-Germanic *mēdwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂met- (“to mow, reap”), enlargement of *h₂meh₁-.
meadow.g: A field or pasture; a piece of land either intentionally cultivated with grass or (especially) naturally covered with grass, especially one

meal.e: From Middle English mel, from Old English mǣl (“measure, time, occasion, set time, time for eating, meal”), from Proto-West Germanic *māl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlą, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”).
meal.g: Food that is prepared and eaten, usually at a specific time, and usually in a comparatively large quantity.

meal.e: From Middle English mele, from Old English melu (“meal, flour”), from Proto-West Germanic *melu, from Proto-Germanic *melwą (“meal, flour”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, mill”).
meal.g: The ground-up edible part of various grains, used as a basis of food or feed; either flour or a coarser blend than flour (usage varies).

mealtime.e: From Middle English meeltime, from Old English mǣltīma (“mealtime”), equivalent to meal + time.
mealtime.g: The appointed time at which a meal is served or eaten.

mean.e: From Middle English menen (“to intend; remember; lament; comfort”), from Old English mǣnan (“to mean, complain”), Proto-West Germanic *mainijan, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; complain”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyn- (“to think”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meyno-, extended form of Proto-Indo-European *mey-.

From Middle English mene, imene, from Old English mǣne, ġemǣne (“common, public, general, universal”), from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī, from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz (“common”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to change, exchange, share”). For a similar change in definition, see vulgar.

meaning.e: From Middle English mening, menyng, equivalent to mean + -ing.
meaning.g: The denotation, referent, or idea connected with a word, expression, or symbol.

means.e: From mean (“method or course of action used to achieve some result”).
means.g: An instrument or condition to achieve a result.

meantime.e: From Middle English menetime, equivalent to mean + time. Adverb is by ellipsis from in the meantime.
meantime.g: The time spent waiting for another event; time in between.

measure.e: From Middle English mesure, from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“a measure”), mētior (“to measure”, supine stem in mēns-) + -tūra. Largely displaced native Old English metan ("to measure" whence modern mete) and ġemet (“a measure”).

meat.e: From Middle English mete (“food”), from Old English mete (“food”), from Proto-West Germanic *mati (“food”), from Proto-Germanic *matiz (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to be wet; grease, fat”). A -ja- derivation from the same base is found in Middle Dutch and Middle Low German met (“lean pork”).
meat.g: The flesh (muscle tissue) of a killed animal used as food.

meddle.e: From Middle English medlen, from Anglo-Norman medler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin misceō (“to mix”).
meddle.g: To interfere in or with; to concern oneself with unduly.

meddler.e: From Middle English medlere, medelere, equivalent to meddle + -er.
meddler.g: One who meddles or interferes in something not of their concern.

mediator.e: From Middle English mediatour, mediatoure, mediatur, medyatour, from Middle French mediateur, mediatur or its etymon Latin mediātor (“one who mediates”), from mediātum, supine of mediō (“be in the middle”), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, mediate + -or.
mediator.g: One who negotiates between parties seeking mutual agreement.

medicine.e: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”).
medicine.g: A substance which specifically promotes healing when ingested or consumed in some way; a pharmaceutical drug.

meditate.e: Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
meditate.g: To contemplate; to keep the mind fixed upon something; to study.

meditation.e: From Old French meditacion, from Latin meditatio, from meditatus, the past participle of meditārī (“to meditate, to think over, consider”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, limit, consider, advise”).
meditation.g: A devotional exercise of, or leading to, contemplation.

medium.e: Borrowed from Latin medium, neuter of medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”).
medium.g: The material of the surrounding environment, e.g. solid, liquid, gas, vacuum, or a specific substance such as a solvent.

meek.e: From Middle English meek, meke, meoc, probably a borrowing from Old Norse mjúkr (“soft; meek”), from Proto-Germanic *meukaz, *mūkaz (“soft; supple”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewg-, *mewk- (“slick, slippery; to slip”); compare Old English smēag (“subtle, stealthy, etc.”) and smūgan.
meek.g: Humble, non-boastful, modest, meager, or self-effacing.

meekly.e: From Middle English mekely, mekeliche, equivalent to meek + -ly.
meekly.g: In a meek manner; quietly and humbly.

meekness.e: From Middle English mekenesse, meknes, meocnesse; equivalent to meek + -ness.
meekness.g: The state or quality of being meek.

meet.e: From Middle English meten, from Old English mētan (“to meet, find, encounter”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtijan (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to come, meet”).
meet.g: To make contact (with someone) while in proximity.

meet.e: From Middle English mete, imete, from Old English ġemǣte (“suitable, having the same measurements”), from the Proto-Germanic *gamētijaz, *mētiz (“reasonable; estimable”) (cognate with Dutch meten (“measure”), German gemäß (“suitable”) etc.), itself from collective prefix *ga- + Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).

meeting.e: From Middle English metynge, metinde, metand, from Old English mētende, *ġemētende, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), equivalent to meet + -ing.

melodious.e: From Middle English melodious, from Middle French melodieus, melodieux. By surface analysis, melod(i) + -ous.
melodious.g: Having a pleasant melody or sound; tuneful.

melody.e: From Middle English melodie, melodye, from Old French melodie, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).
melody.g: A sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase.

melon.e: From Middle English meloun, melon, from Old French melon, from Late Latin melonem, from Latin melopeponem, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).
melon.g: Some of the plants of the family Cucurbitaceae grown for food, generally not including the cucumber.

melt.e: From Middle English melten, from a merger of Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both meaning “to melt, digest,” from Proto-West Germanic *meltan and *maltijan, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną and *maltijaną, both from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“melt”).
melt.g: To change (or to be changed) from a solid state to a liquid state, usually by a gradual heat.

member.e: From Middle English membre, from Old French membre, from Latin membrum (“limb, body part”), from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Coexists with native limb, from Old English lim (“limb, joint, main branch”). Mostly displaced lith (“limb, joint, member”).
member.g: One who belongs to a group.

memorial.e: From Late Latin memoriale, neuter of memorialis. By surface analysis, memory + -ial.

memory.e: From Anglo-Norman memorie, Old French memoire etc., from Latin memoria (“the faculty of remembering, remembrance, memory, a historical account”), from memor (“mindful, remembering”).
memory.g: The ability of the brain to record information or impressions with the facility of recalling them later, usually at will.

men.e: From Middle English men, from Old English menn (“people”), from Proto-Germanic *manniz, nominative plural of Proto-Germanic *mann- (“person”).

mend.e: From Middle English menden (“to cure; to do good to, benefit; to do or make better, improve; to get better, recover; to keep in a good state; to put right, amend; to reform, repent”), the aphetic form of amenden (“to alter, change (especially for the better); to atone; to chastise, punish; to correct, remedy, amend; to cure; to excel, surpass; to forgive.
mend.g: To physically repair (something that is broken, defaced, decayed, torn, or otherwise damaged).

mend.e: Partly: (chiefly etymology 2 sense 2 (“recompense; restoration or reparation”)) from Middle English mend, mende (“cure, remedy; damages, recompense; atonement; penance; relief”), the aphetic form of amende, amendes (“retribution, amends; a fine; atonement; penance”) (though attested slightly earlier).
mend.g: Senses relating to improvement or repairing.

menstrual.e: From Middle English menstruall, from Latin mēnstruālis, from mēnstrua (“menses”), from neuter plural of mēnstruus (“of a month, monthly, of menstruation”), from mēnsis (“month”) + -ālis (“-al”); see moon.
menstrual.g: Of or relating to the menses.

menstruate.e: From menstruum + -ate (verb-forming suffix); sense 2 (“to undergo menstruation”) is possibly a back-formation from menstruation.
menstruate.g: To stain with or as if with menses.

menstruation.e: From menstruum + -ation, modelled after Late Latin menstruatio. The word is a cognate with French menstruation, Spanish menstruación, which displaced Old English mōnaþblōd (literally “monthblood”).
menstruation.g: The periodic discharging of the menses, the flow of blood and cells from the lining of the uterus in unfertilized females of humans and othe

menstruous.e: From Anglo-Norman menstruus, Middle French menstrueus, and their source, Late Latin menstruosus (“menstruating”), from Latin mēnstruum.
menstruous.g: Of or pertaining to menstruation; menstrual.

mention.e: From Middle English mencioun, mention, from Old French mention, from Latin mentiōnem, accusative of mentiō (“a mention, calling to mind”).
mention.g: A speaking or noticing of anything, usually in a brief or cursory manner.

mentor.e: From French mentor, from Ancient Greek Μέντωρ (Méntōr, “Mentor”), a mythological character in the Odyssey, whose name, a historical name from Ancient Greece, shares the same root as English mind.
mentor.g: A wise and trusted counselor or teacher.

meon.e: From Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size.

mercenary.e: From Middle English mercenarye (“someone paid to work, hireling”), from Latin mercēnārius (“hired for money”), from mercēs (“reward, wages, price”).
mercenary.g: One motivated by gain, especially monetary.

merchandise.e: From Middle English marchaundise (“commerce, trading; buying; business transaction, deal; merchandise, goods, wares; possessions”), from Anglo-Norman marchaundise and Old French marcheandise (modern French marchandise), from Old French marcheant (“seller, vendor”) (ultimately from Latin mercātus (“buying and selling, trade, traffic; market.
merchandise.g: Goods which are or were offered or intended for sale.

merchandise.e: From Middle English marchaundisen (“to engage in commerce, traffic”), from marchaundise (noun) (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs).
merchandise.g: To engage in trade; to carry on commerce.

merchant.e: From Middle English marchaunt, from Anglo-Norman marchaunt, from mercans, from the verb mercor (“to trade, deal, sell”).
merchant.g: A person who traffics in commodities for profit.

merciful.e: From Middle English merciful, mercyful, equivalent to mercy + -ful.

merciless.e: From Middle English merciles, mercyles, equivalent to mercy + -less.
merciless.g: Showing no mercy; cruel and pitiless.

mercy.e: From Middle English mercy, merci, from Anglo-Norman merci (compare continental Old French merci, mercit), from Latin mercēs (“wages, fee, price”), from merx (“wares, merchandise”).
mercy.g: Relenting; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.

mere.e: From Middle English mere, mer, from Anglo-Norman meer, from Old French mier, from Latin merus (“pure, unmixed, undiluted”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to sparkle, gleam”). The Middle English word was perhaps influenced by or conflated with sound-alike Middle English mere (“glorious, noble, splendid, fine, pure”).
mere.g: Just, only; no more than, pure and simple, neither more nor better than might be expected.

mere.e: From Middle English mere, from Old English mǣre, ġemǣre (“boundary; limit”), from Proto-Germanic *mairiją (“boundary”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to fence”).

merely.e: From Middle English mereli, equivalent to mere + -ly.
merely.g: Without any other reason etc.; only, just, and nothing more.

meron.e: From mero- (“part, portion”) + -on. Coined by American scientists Curtis G. Allan Jr., Roger Dashen, and David J. Gross, in 1977.
meron.g: Either of the pair of entities that together make up an instanton.

meron.e: Back-formation from epimeron, ultimately from Ancient Greek μῆρος (mêros, “thigh”).
meron.g: A sclerite on the side of the thorax of an insect, above the coxae of the mid and hind legs.

merrily.e: From Middle English myriely, from Old English myriġlīċe; equivalent to merry + -ly.
merrily.g: In a cheerful or merry way.

merry.e: From Middle English myrie, merie, mery, from Old English myrġe, myriġe (“pleasing, agreeable; pleasant, sweet, delightful; melodious”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgī (“short, slow, leisurely”), from Proto-Germanic *murguz (“short, slow”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short”).
merry.g: Jolly and full of high spirits; happy.

merrymaker.g: One who makes merry; a reveler or celebrant.

mesh.e: From Middle English mesche, from Old English masc (“net”) (perhaps influenced in form by related Old English mæscre (“mesh, spot”)), from the related Proto-Germanic *maskwǭ and *maskrǭ respectively, from Proto-Indo-European *mezg- (“to knit, twist, plait”).
mesh.g: A structure made of connected strands of metal, fiber, or other flexible/ductile material, with evenly spaced openings between them.

mess.e: Perhaps a corruption of Middle English mesh (“mash”), compare muss, or derived from Etymology 2 "mixed foods, as for animals".
mess.g: A thing or group of things in a disagreeable, disorganised, or dirty state; hence a bad situation.

mess.e: From Middle English mes, partly from Old English mēse, mēose (“table”), a vernacular loan from Latin/Late Latin mē(n)sa (“table; meal”); and partly from Old French mes, Late Latin missum, from mittō (“to put, place (e.g. on the table)”).

message.e: From Middle English message, from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”). Partially displaced Old English ærende (whence errand).
message.g: A communication, or what is communicated; any concept or information conveyed.

messenger.e: From Middle English messengere, messingere, messangere, from Old French messanger, a variant of Old French messagier (French messager), equivalent to message + -er. For the replacement of -ager with -enger, -inger, -anger, compare passenger, harbinger, scavenger, porringer.

met.e: From Middle English meten (“to dream”), from Old English mætan (“to dream”).
met.g: To dream; to occur (to one) in a dream.

metal.e: From Middle English metal, a borrowing from Old French metal, from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).
metal.g: Chemical elements or alloys, their ores, and the mines where their ores come from.

mete.e: From Middle English meten, from Old English metan (“to measure, mete out, mark off, compare, estimate; pass over, traverse”), from Proto-West Germanic *metan, from Proto-Germanic *metaną (“to measure”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, consider”).
mete.g: To dispense, measure in order to dispense, allot (especially punishment, reward etc.).

mete.e: From Middle English mete, imete, from Old English mǣte, ġemǣte (“moderate, suitable”).

meteyard.g: A yard, staff, or rod used as a measuring device.

manservant.e: From Middle English man servant, man servaunt; equivalent to man + servant.
